column3: A Tibetan Buddhist temple built in the 16th century in Hohhot, with a silver Buddha and richly painted halls. It was the first major lamasery here.
The grave mound of Wang Zhaojun, a Han court lady who married a Xiongnu chief to bring peace. A green hill rises from the plain.
A museum with dinosaur skeletons, Mongolian costumes and relics of the steppe peoples, with a striking modern building.
A temple of the Yellow Hat sect of Tibetan Buddhism in Hohhot, with an old hall of Ming-era design.
A temple with a base topped by five small pagodas, covered in thousands of tiny Buddha carvings and a Mongolian star chart.
A mountain range north of Hohhot, with forests and meadows, a green backdrop for the city.
Steamed dumplings stuffed with lamb, with thin, frilly wrappers, a Hohhot classic, often eaten with milk tea.
Mutton boiled with only salt and eaten by hand, cut off the bone with a knife. This is the classic way to eat on the Mongolian steppe.
Salty milk tea is made with brick tea and milk, often with millet and fried snacks, and is the Mongolian welcome drink.
A dried cheese made from milk that is sweet and sour, a staple snack that herders carry on the grasslands.
Noodles made from oat flour, which are rolled into thin tubes and steamed, a hearty staple of the cool northern plateau.
A mildly alcoholic drink made by fermenting mare's milk, an old Mongolian tradition, and served at festivals.
The big summer festival of wrestling, archery and horse racing, held on the grasslands for centuries. Families gather in colorful dress.
The morin khuur is a two-stringed fiddle with a carved horse head, whose deep, soft voice is the sound of the steppe.
Khoomei, or throat singing, is a technique in which one singer makes two notes at the same time, a low drone and high whistling melody.
A round tent covered with felt over a wooden frame that can be taken down and moved, the traditional home of herders.
The largest Tibetan Buddhist monastery in Inner Mongolia, with white buildings that climb a hillside in a mountain valley.
A memorial hall for Genghis Khan, in the Ordos grassland. It holds no body but is a place of worship for Mongols.
Baotou's lamb comes from grassland sheep, with a mild taste, and is boiled, roasted or served in hotpot.
Steamed lamb dumplings from Baotou with a juicy filling, a staple breakfast food.
A tall dune in the Kubuqi Desert that makes a low humming sound when sand slides down. Visitors can ride camels or slide on sleds.
A grand memorial complex in Mongolian style, with domed halls and a great statue, where rituals have been held for centuries.
Lamb from the Ordos steppe, with tender, clean-tasting meat, is a regional pride.
Mutton boiled and eaten by hand, cut off the bone, with salt and perhaps a dip of chives.
One of the best grasslands in the world, with rolling green hills, herds of horses and sheep, and big skies, and wildflowers bloom in summer.
A border town facing Russia, with a bright gate, Russian-style buildings and shops with nesting dolls.
A forested area with hot springs, volcanic lakes and mountain views, a gentle summer escape.
A large lake on the Hulunbuir grassland, one of the biggest in northern China, rich in fish and home to many birds.
A whole lamb roasted until the skin is crisp, then carved at the table, a feast for guests and celebrations.
Round loaves of Russian-style bread are baked in the border town, thanks to the Russian settlers' influence.
A people of herders and hunters in the Hulunbuir area, known for their reindeer and for their traditions.
A heap of stones, branches and prayer flags built on a hill as a shrine, where people walk around three times to ask for blessings.
A geopark with granite rock forests, volcanic landforms and grasslands, a varied landscape in Chifeng.
A big salt lake on the steppe where swans, cranes and other birds rest on their migration.
Meat grilled over charcoal on the table, an Inner Mongolian barbecue tradition, with a dipping sauce.
Oat noodles steamed in rolls or tubes, and eaten with a savory sauce, a staple of the dry north.
Sweet grapes grown in the dry climate near the Yellow River, ripe in autumn.
Beef raised on dry grassland in Wuhai, lean and tasty, often dried or braised.
A sweet, fragrant melon grown on the Hetao Plain by the Yellow River, where long hours of sun make it extra sweet.
Lamb from the Hetao Plain, known for its tender meat that has little gamey smell.
A desert with the tallest stationary dunes in the world, some almost 500 meters high, with small lakes between them.
The ruins of a fortress city of the Western Xia and Yuan dynasties, which was abandoned in the 14th century and left in the desert.
Cistanche is a desert herb that grows on the roots of saxaul trees, which is used in tonics and is known as desert ginseng.
Milk from Bactrian camels, which is thick and slightly salty, a traditional drink in the Gobi.
A wide grassland with rivers and herds of horses, a quiet area with big skies.
Lamb raised on the Xilingol grassland, known for tender meat and no strong smell, and one of the best in China.
A grassland in eastern Inner Mongolia, with a long Mongolian tradition and wrestling, and in summer, it is bright green.
Yellow millet from Tongliao, which cooks into a sticky, sweet porridge or cake.
Potatoes grown on the cool plateau, with a rich, floury texture. Ulanqab is a major potato-growing region.
Rice grown on the plains of the Hinggan League, where short summers and cold nights give it a sweet taste.
